analysis.one_liner: Lifts all federal campaign contribution limits while requiring instant online disclosure of donations.
analysis.headline: All 73 of the bill's cosponsors were House Republicans; it never received a hearing or vote and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended, after 2002, every legal limit on how much money a donor can give to a federal candidate. It would also have shut down the presidential public financing system, where taxpayers check a box to send $3 to fund campaigns, and required campaigns to report every contribution online within 24 hours. One section would have barred labor unions from spending any member dues on political activity unless each person gave written permission.
analysis.who_benefits: Large donors, who could give unlimited sums directly to candidates and parties after 2002. National parties would gain a far larger pool of money, and campaigns would no longer depend on many small donations. Candidates who can attract a few very large checks would benefit most.

how_it_helps.text: After calendar year 2002, none of the existing limits on contributions to federal candidates would apply, so a single donor could give a candidate any amount [S2] [S3].

Campaigns would have to file all reports electronically and place them on the internet, and would have to notify regulators of any contribution received in the final 90 days of a campaign within 24 hours [S3].

National party committees would have to report all funds transferred to state and local party committees, even money not otherwise treated as a contribution, which would expose soft money flows [S2] [S3].
The bill's stated aim was to let challengers compete with incumbents by making it easier to raise money quickly, and to replace limits with full, immediate disclosure [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary donors and voters would lose relative political influence to the biggest checkbooks, taxpayers would lose the $3 checkoff that funds presidential campaigns, and labor unions would be barred from using dues for any political purpose without a written authorization from each person.

drawbacks.text: Removing all contribution limits means one wealthy donor could give a candidate as much money as tens of thousands of small donors combined, magnifying the political voice of a small group of very large givers [S2] [S3].

The bill terminates the Presidential Election Campaign Fund and the taxpayer checkoff that financed it, ending the one system that let small donors fund presidential candidates without any contribution at all; leftover money would go to the general treasury [S2] [S3].

The labor provision would make it unlawful for unions to collect any dues used for political activity without separate prior written authorization from each person, which unions argued would sharply curtail their ability to speak politically on behalf of working people [S3].
Even with unlimited money legal, reporting every contribution within 24 hours and strictly identifying all donors over $200 would impose real compliance burdens on campaigns and treasurers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The disclosure half of the bill was genuinely strong: 24-hour electronic reporting of every late contribution and public tracking of party soft money would have given voters information they did not have. But the centerpiece, unlimited contributions, would trade the appearance of fairness for a system where the largest donors dominate even more openly, and it would eliminate rather than reform public financing. The bill acknowledged this trade openly, betting that instant disclosure would police the money. Many campaign finance scholars doubted that disclosure alone checks the influence of six- and seven-figure checks.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. John Doolittle introduced the bill on April 4, 2001, joined by House leaders Tom DeLay and Dick Armey and dozens of other Republicans [S3].
The bill was referred to the Committee on House Administration and to the Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
Seventy-three House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans [S4].
No action beyond the initial referral is recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, existing contribution limits and the presidential public financing checkoff remained in place through this Congress, and large donors did not gain the right to give unlimited amounts. The disclosure improvements it offered were also lost, though separate bipartisan campaign finance legislation was moving in the same period.

for.name: Rep. John T. Doolittle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would lift all federal contribution limits, end presidential public financing, and require 24-hour electronic disclosure [S1] [S3].

for.name: 73 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Majority Leader Dick Armey and Majority Whip Tom DeLay [S3] [S4].

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Primary committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never reported the bill or scheduled a markup [S5].

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Secondary committee of referral for the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for the provisions terminating the presidential campaign fund and never acted on them [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 73 cosponsors was a House Republican; it was offered as the Republican alternative to the bipartisan Shays-Meehan campaign finance bill that was moving through the same Congress.

industries.note: After 2002 the bill would have removed every cap on contributions, letting a single donor give unlimited sums directly to candidates. That gain comes directly at the cost of ordinary donors' relative influence over elections.

Unions would be barred from collecting any dues used for political activity unless each member signed a separate written authorization, covering not just elections but lobbying and even educating members about federal legislation. Supporters called it consent protection; unions viewed it as a curb on working people's collective political voice.

Parties would gain access to unlimited donations once limits ended, but would have to report every dollar transferred to state and local committees, exposing their soft money flows. The added money would far outweigh the added paperwork.

Unlimited contributions would expand the pool of money available for paid ads and consultants, since campaigns could raise far larger sums from the biggest donors. More spending means more revenue for those who sell campaign services.
